source_refs.note: Topic 20.1.2 with Table 20.1 and Quick Check 20.1, answered (PDF 61-62); the second Figure 20.1 is redrawn. The book labels the C-H bonds 'sp2-sp2'; hydrogen uses its 1s orbital, so the figure says sp2-s. Answers need review.

blocks.text: The hexagonal framework of benzene is explained by hybridisation. Each carbon is sp2 hybridised: of its three sp2 orbitals, two form sigma bonds with the neighbouring carbons and one with a hydrogen atom. All the sp2 orbitals lie in one plane, so all the carbon and hydrogen atoms of this sigma framework are in the same plane, at 120 degrees.

Each carbon also has one unhybridised 2p orbital, perpendicular to the sigma framework. The six p orbitals are parallel and overlap sideways with both neighbours, forming a pi electron cloud above and below the plane of the ring; the molecule is conjugated. The six pi electrons are shared equally by all six carbons: they are delocalised. As a result all six C-C bonds have the same length, 139 pm, and benzene is drawn as a hexagon with a circle inside, the circle standing for the delocalised pi electrons.

blocks.alt: Three panels. (a) A flat hexagon of carbon atoms, each bonded to a hydrogen, labelled C-C sp2-sp2 sigma and C-H sp2-s sigma, all at 120 degrees. (b) The ring seen from the side with an upright p orbital, two lobes, on every carbon. (c) Two rings of pi electron density, one above and one below the ring of carbons.
blocks.caption: Sigma framework, p orbitals and the delocalised pi system of benzene (original diagram after the book's second Figure 20.1).
blocks.long_description: The sigma bonds hold the six carbons and six hydrogens in a flat ring. Above and below this ring each carbon has a p orbital; because the ring is flat, every p orbital overlaps equally with both neighbours. The result is a continuous ring of pi electron density above the plane and another below it.

items: The delocalisation (resonance) energy of benzene is about 152 kJ/mol. What does this mean, and how does it affect benzene's reactivity?
X-ray studies show benzene is planar. If it were not planar, how would its reactivity differ?
Why are all the bonds in the benzene ring the same length?
How does the atomic orbital picture explain the delocalisation of pi electrons in benzene?
